Chlordiazepoxide: Benzodiazepine (long-acting anxiolytic); Amitriptyline Hydrochloride: Tricyclic antidepressant (TCA)
Psychotropic substance under the NDPS Act, 1985 and Schedule H/H1 of the Drugs & Cosmetics Rules; Amitriptyline Hydrochloride: Schedule H – prescription only
sections: Yellow crystalline powder (base); hydrochloride is soluble in water.
White crystalline powder (hydrochloride), freely soluble in water; melting point 197.5 °C; logP 3.0 at pH 7.4.

Chlordiazepoxide: The first benzodiazepine, discovered by chance by Leo Sternbach at Roche in 1955. First approval/introduction: Patented 1958; approved 1960 (Hoffmann-La Roche). Amitriptyline Hydrochloride: Developed by Merck in the late 1950s; clinical trials showed antidepressant efficacy equivalent to imipramine. On the WHO List of Essential Medicines. First approval/introduction: US FDA 1961 (Merck).
Strength not stated in product list (common: Chlordiazepoxide 5 mg + Amitriptyline
Chlordiazepoxide gives rapid anxiolysis, while amitriptyline provides antidepressant and sleep-promoting effects; useful where anxiety and depression coexist.

Chlordiazepoxide Enhances GABA-A mediated inhibition in the limbic system, reducing anxiety and associated autonomic/visceral symptoms. Receptor / target profile: Acts on benzodiazepine allosteric sites of GABA-A receptors, producing anxiolytic, sedative, anticonvulsant and muscle-relaxant effects.

Amitriptyline Hydrochloride Inhibits neuronal reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin; also antagonises H1, muscarinic and alpha-1 receptors and blocks sodium channels. At low doses it modulates descending pain pathways (analgesic effect independent of mood). Receptor / target profile: Inhibits SERT and NET; potent antagonist at 5-HT2A, 5-HT2C, alpha-1, H1 and M1–M5 receptors; blocks voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels.
Hepatic – to desmethylchlordiazepoxide, demoxepam, desmethyldiazepam, oxazepam
Summary: Well absorbed; Tmax 0.5–4 h. ~96% protein bound. Metabolised to active desmethylchlordiazepoxide, demoxepam and desmethyldiazepam. Half-life 5–30 h (active metabolites much longer).
Hepatic – CYP2D6, CYP2C19, CYP3A4 (active metabolite nortriptyline)
Summary: Well absorbed; Tmax 2–12 h. ~95% protein bound. Metabolised by CYP2D6/2C19 to active nortriptyline. Half-life 10–28 h.

Mixed anxiety–depression with somatic symptoms (including functional GI disorders)
One tablet two to three times daily, or at bedtime; adjust as directed (max equivalent of chlordiazepoxide 40 mg + amitriptyline 100 mg/day)
Review after 2–4 weeks; avoid prolonged benzodiazepine exposure
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.
Use the lowest dose (5 mg two to four times daily max); avoid where possible (Beers list).

Not recommended under 16 years for depression; used for enuresis (≥6 y) in some regions.

Amitriptyline Hydrochloride: Take at bedtime; avoid alcohol.
Amitriptyline Hydrochloride: ECG (QRS/QTc) if cardiac disease or >100 mg/day; plasma levels in overdose risk; weight.

Chlordiazepoxide: Somnolence, confusion, respiratory depression, coma. Supportive care; flumazenil with caution. Amitriptyline Hydrochloride: Life-threatening: arrhythmias, QRS widening, hypotension, seizures, coma, anticholinergic toxicity. ECG monitoring; sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening; supportive care.
Controlled trials in the 1970s (e.g. Feighner et al., 1979) showed the combination was superior to either component for mixed anxiety–depression in the first weeks.
Take in the evening – causes drowsiness
Dry mouth and constipation are common
Keep out of reach – overdose is dangerous
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
